about: Applied Knowledge Test Paper 2 (MBBS0085) is the second of the two end-of-year examinations in UCL's MBBS Year 1, not a taught module. UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 Format of Assessments describes it, like Paper 1, as a 2-hour online integrated paper of no more than 100 marks, mixing single best answer and very short answer questions, some with images, with no negative marking. Some UCL documents label the code as the Clinical and Professional Skills Assessment (CPSA), so confirm details with the Medical School. In the May 2026 dates list it falls on 20 May 2027, two days after Paper 1. This guide explains what is confirmed and how to prepare; it does not invent a syllabus.

notes.h: What AKT Paper 2 is and what is confirmed about it
notes.body:
Applied Knowledge Test Paper 2 (MBBS0085) is an examination at the end of UCL's MBBS Year 1, not a taught module, so it has no syllabus of its own. It tests applied knowledge from across the whole year.

What UCL's 2026–27 documents say
- The Year 1 Format of Assessments (2026–27, August 2026 version) describes the summative assessment as an integrated written and practical assessment made up of two Applied Knowledge Tests (AKTs): Paper 1 (MBBS0084) and Paper 2 (MBBS0085).
- Paper 2, like Paper 1, is a 2-hour online paper worth no more than 100 marks, with a mix of single best answer (SBA) and very short answer (VSA) questions, some of which may include images.
- There is no negative marking.
- The papers are blueprinted to the year of study, the MBBS Curriculum Map, and the GMC's Good medical practice and Outcomes for graduates as relevant to this stage. They aim to test intellectual and practical skills rather than simple recall, across modules and disciplines, including Clinical and Professional Practice teaching.
- Sample questions are on the Assessment Unit's Moodle site.

Dates (check for changes)
- UCL's 2026–27 assessment dates list (May 2026 version) gives AKT 2 on Thursday 20 May 2027 at 14:30, two days after AKT 1 on Tuesday 18 May 2027.
- The same list gives late summer sittings of AKT 1 and AKT 2 on 4 and 5 August 2027.
- Always confirm against the latest version from the Medical School.

A naming point that can confuse
Different UCL pages label this code differently. The module catalogue's listing and the Year 1 programme page call it Applied Knowledge Test Paper 2, but the programme page's link and the Format of Assessments label the code "CPSA" (Clinical and Professional Skills Assessment). The 2026–27 MBBS Mark Scheme also says the assessments in Years 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 comprise an Applied Knowledge Test and a Clinical and Professional Skills Assessment. However, the Year 1 Format of Assessments describes MBBS0085 itself as a 2-hour online SBA/VSA paper, the same format as Paper 1. UCL also posted a revised Year 1 Format of Assessments (v2, September 2026), which could not be checked for this guide. If you are unsure what Paper 2 covers or how the two papers are combined, ask the Year 1 assessment team rather than relying on rumours.

What else the official documents say
- The 2026–27 MBBS Mark Scheme states that the AKT pass mark is set by standard setting using a modified Angoff method, in which judges estimate how a borderline candidate would perform on each question.
- It also states that pass results in individual components are carried forward to in-year resit sittings.

What they do not say
They do not say how the marks of Papers 1 and 2 are combined, which topics each paper samples, or the pass mark itself. Read the documents UCL names for candidates: the Examination Guide for Candidates, the Medical School's policies for MBBS assessments and the MBBS Mark Scheme.

Exam tips: put both AKT dates, times and rules in your calendar as soon as they are confirmed, and do the sample questions on Moodle so the online platform holds no surprises.

notes.h: Question formats: what is and is not stated
notes.body:
Both Year 1 AKT papers mix single best answer (SBA) and very short answer (VSA) questions, and some include images. It is worth being precise about what UCL has actually published.

What is stated, and for which papers
- For the summative AKTs, the 2026–27 Year 1 Format of Assessments says only that each paper is a mixture of SBA and VSA questions, may include images and has no negative marking.
- For the formative papers in the November and February Consolidation, Integration and Feedback (CIF) weeks, the same document says SBA questions each have five options and VSA questions require an answer of no more than five words. The document does not repeat these limits for the summative papers.
- The formative papers are designed to give you experience of all the question types used in the summative assessments, so practising in the formative format is sensible. Check the instructions on the summative paper itself, and the sample questions on Moodle, for the exact rules on the day.

SBA technique
- Read the lead-in (the question at the end of the stem) first, so you know whether it asks for a mechanism, a diagnosis, a structure, an investigation or the next step.
- Read the stem actively: age, sex, timing, key positive and negative findings, and any results.
- Predict an answer before looking at the options.
- Several options may be partly true; pick the one that best fits every feature of the stem. Watch words such as "most likely", "first", "most appropriate" and "least".

VSA technique
- You must produce the answer without options, so practise recall rather than recognition.
- Give one specific answer, spelled correctly; do not hedge with a list of alternatives.
- Answer exactly what is asked: if the question asks for a cell, name the cell, not the molecule it secretes.
- A good drill is to cover the options of an SBA and answer it as a VSA.

Images
- Expect possibilities such as anatomy specimens and diagrams, radiographs and other images, histology, data plots and ECG-type traces.
- First name what you are looking at: the modality or stain, the view or plane, and the orientation. For graphs, read the axes and units before the curve.

Timing and marking
- 2 hours for up to 100 marks is about 1.2 minutes per mark. Do a first pass answering everything you can, flag hard questions and return to them.
- With no negative marking, never leave an answer blank.

Exam tips: treat the five-option and five-word formats as how the formative papers work, not as a promise about the summative paper; read the instructions on the day.

notes.h: Preparing for the second paper of the week
notes.body:
In the 2026–27 dates list, Paper 2 comes two days after Paper 1. That makes the week as much a test of stamina and recovery as of knowledge.

Before exam week
- Revise the whole year. UCL's documents do not say that either paper is limited to particular modules, so do not gamble on topics being "Paper 1 only".
- Use the Year 1 learning objectives on Moodle and the MBBS Curriculum Map as your checklist, rating each objective red, amber or green.
- Use retrieval practice (questions and flashcards) and spaced review rather than rereading; mix topics within each session, because integrated papers mix them.
- Analyse your CIF formative results, especially the February mock taken under exam conditions: classify each error as a knowledge gap, misreading, technique or timing problem.
- Do at least two full 2-hour timed practice sessions on consecutive or alternate days to rehearse the rhythm of exam week.

Between Paper 1 and Paper 2
- Do not hold a detailed post-mortem of Paper 1 with friends. You cannot change it, and it costs you sleep and confidence.
- Spend the gap on light, high-yield review: your own summary sheets, flagged weak areas, and a short set of mixed questions to keep retrieval sharp.
- Prioritise sleep, food and a little exercise. Tiredness damages reading accuracy, which matters greatly in SBA questions.
- Re-check the time: in the May 2026 version of the dates list, Paper 2 is in the afternoon (14:30), while Paper 1 is in the morning.

On the day
- Arrive or log in early and follow the online exam instructions exactly.
- Use the same routine that worked in Paper 1: lead-in first, predict, choose, flag, return.
- If one topic goes badly, move on; each question carries its own marks.

Integration practice
Take a common scenario and work through it from every angle. For example, a patient with pneumonia: the organism and how it causes disease, innate and adaptive immunity, lung anatomy and imaging, gas exchange, the principles of how antibiotics act, interpretation of blood results, communicating with the patient and the ethics of consent. Paper 2 can draw on any of these.

If things go wrong
If illness or personal circumstances affect your preparation or performance, find out about UCL's extenuating circumstances process before the exam, and talk to your personal tutor or Medical Student Support. The 2026–27 dates list includes late summer sittings in August 2027.

Exam tips: plan exam week in advance (sleep, meals, travel or log-in, review sheets) so that the two-day gap is used for recovery and light review, not panic.

The questions in this pack are practice items in the formats UCL uses in its Year 1 formative papers (five-option SBAs and very short answers). They are not taken from UCL papers, and the official documents do not list the content of each AKT paper, so use the Year 1 learning objectives to check coverage. These items cover infection and immunity, acid–base physiology, data interpretation and law, complementing the practice in the Paper 1 pack.

High-yield facts behind these questions
- Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for the bicarbonate buffer: pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻] ÷ (0.23 × PaCO₂)), with bicarbonate in mmol/L and PaCO₂ in kPa. The factor 0.23 (approximately) converts PaCO₂ in kPa into dissolved CO₂ in mmol/L; with PaCO₂ in mmHg the factor is about 0.03. A normal arterial pH is roughly 7.35 to 7.45.
- Worked example: bicarbonate 24 mmol/L and PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa give 0.23 × 5.3 ≈ 1.22, and 24 ÷ 1.22 ≈ 19.7, so pH ≈ 6.1 + 1.29 ≈ 7.39.
- Diagnostic tests: sensitivity = true positives ÷ all with the disease; specificity = true negatives ÷ all without the disease; positive predictive value = true positives ÷ all positive results; negative predictive value = true negatives ÷ all negative results. Predictive values change with prevalence; sensitivity and specificity do not, in principle.
- Staphylococci are Gram-positive cocci in clusters and catalase-positive; Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase-positive, while S. epidermidis is coagulase-negative. Streptococci form chains or pairs and are catalase-negative.
- Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales), section 1 principles: a person is assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it; they are not treated as unable to decide until all practicable steps to help them have failed; an unwise decision does not by itself mean lack of capacity; anything done for a person who lacks capacity must be in their best interests; and the least restrictive option should be considered. Capacity is specific to the decision and the time.
- Plasma cells secrete antibody; IgG crosses the placenta; Toll-like receptor 4 recognises lipopolysaccharide.

How to use the questions
- Answer each SBA before looking at the options, then read why every other option is wrong; distractors are built from common mistakes.
- Answer the VSA items from memory in a few words.
- For calculations, write the formula and units first.

Exam tips: in calculation SBAs, most wrong options come from a unit slip, an inverted ratio or using the wrong formula, so check each of these before you commit.

cards.b: pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻] ÷ (0.23 × PaCO₂)), HCO₃⁻ in mmol/L, PaCO₂ in kPa.
Sensitivity: true positives ÷ all with disease. Specificity: true negatives ÷ all without disease.
…does not by itself mean that a person lacks capacity (section 1(4)).

questions.q: An arterial blood sample shows bicarbonate 24 mmol/L and PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa. Using pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻] ÷ (0.23 × PaCO₂)), what is the pH (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.why: 0.23 × 5.3 ≈ 1.22, and 24 ÷ 1.22 ≈ 19.7, whose log₁₀ is about 1.29, so pH ≈ 6.1 + 1.29 = 7.39. 6.76 leaves out the 0.23 factor and divides bicarbonate by PaCO₂ directly. 4.81 inverts the ratio, putting dissolved CO₂ over bicarbonate. 8.28 uses the mmHg factor 0.03 with a PaCO₂ in kPa. 9.08 uses the natural logarithm instead of log₁₀.

questions.q: A new test is used on 200 people who have a disease and 800 who do not. It is positive in 180 of those with the disease and negative in 760 of those without. What is its sensitivity?
questions.why: Sensitivity = true positives ÷ all with the disease = 180 ÷ 200 = 90%. 95% is the specificity, 760 ÷ 800. 81.8% is the positive predictive value, 180 ÷ (180 + 40), because 40 of the 800 without the disease tested positive. 97.4% is the negative predictive value, 760 ÷ (760 + 20). 18% divides the 180 true positives by all 1000 people tested, which is not a test accuracy measure.

questions.q: A blood culture grows Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase-positive and coagulase-positive. What is the most likely organism?
questions.why: Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase-positive are staphylococci, and coagulase-positivity identifies S. aureus. S. epidermidis is also a catalase-positive staphylococcus but is coagulase-negative. Streptococcus pyogenes forms chains and is catalase-negative. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a catalase-negative diplococcus. Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus, so it fails at the first step.

questions.q: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales), which statement is one of the Act's principles?
options: The next of kin can consent to treatment for any adult who lacks capacity
A person who makes an unwise decision should be treated as lacking capacity
A person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it
Once capacity has been assessed, the result applies to all later decisions
A person with a diagnosis of dementia lacks capacity
questions.why: Section 1(2) sets out the presumption of capacity. The Act says the opposite of the unwise-decision statement: an unwise decision alone does not show lack of capacity. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, so one assessment does not cover all later decisions. Lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a condition such as dementia; the person's ability to make the particular decision must be assessed. Next of kin cannot consent on an adult's behalf unless they hold a relevant lasting power of attorney or are a court-appointed deputy; otherwise decisions are made in the person's best interests.

questions.q: VSA practice (answer each in a few words): (a) Name the cell that secretes antibody. (b) Name the antibody class that crosses the placenta. (c) Name the Toll-like receptor that recognises lipopolysaccharide.
UCL's 2026–27 dates list puts AKT Paper 2 two days after Paper 1. Describe four things you would do to perform well in Paper 2.
markScheme: Revise the whole year rather than guessing which topics fall in which paper
Avoid a detailed post-mortem of Paper 1; focus forward
Use the gap for sleep, food, exercise and light high-yield review or a short mixed question set
Check the time and log-in details (afternoon start in the May 2026 list) and repeat the same exam routine; no blanks as there is no negative marking
questions.modelAnswer: First, I would revise all Year 1 content beforehand, because UCL does not say which topics fall in which paper. Second, after Paper 1 I would avoid going through answers with friends, since it cannot change my mark and would increase anxiety. Third, I would use the two-day gap for sleep, proper meals, some exercise and light review of my summary sheets and a short set of mixed questions to keep recall sharp. Fourth, I would check the exact time and log-in details, since Paper 2 is listed for the afternoon, and use the same routine as in Paper 1, answering every question because there is no negative marking.
